query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Upon exposure to high temperatures (700–900 °C), the passive film on pre-exposed Q235 steel undergoes a phase transformation from a dense, protective oxide (e.g., Fe3O4-rich phase) to a more porous or less adherent oxide (e.g., FeO or non-stoichiometric phases), leading to rapid corrosion degradation compared to the stable oxide state at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel with a conventionally formed passivation film composed primarily of stable iron oxide phases (as per PMC9504384 and PMC9867134 studies)
generation.intervention: Subject passivated Q235 steel samples to a controlled annealing schedule that mimics high-temperature exposure (e.g., ramp to 750 °C and hold for defined times) versus a control maintained at room temperature, both in the presence of a salt atmosphere
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in the range 700–900 °C under aggressive salt (chloride) environment; comparison with room temperature exposure under identical salt conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Phase composition and microstructural characteristics of the oxide film
generation.mechanism: High-temperature exposure induces phase changes in the oxide film, transforming it into phases with higher porosity and lower adhesion, thus facilitating aggressive ion ingress and rapid corrosion, whereas at room temperature the film remains in its protective phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: XRD and SEM analyses will reveal a distinct phase change in the high-temperature-treated samples (e.g., appearance of porous FeO peaks and microcracks) accompanied by an increase in corrosion rate (e.g., several fold higher mass loss) relative to samples kept at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Passivated Q235 steel exposed to chloride atmosphere at room temperature maintaining a dense, protective oxide film and low corrosion rate
generation.boundary: This mechanism predominates only when the thermal energy is sufficient to drive the phase transformation; at shorter high-temperature exposures or lower temperatures, the film may remain in the protective phase.
generation.uncertainty: The exact phase boundaries, transformation kinetics, and their quantitative impact on corrosion behavior need further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose passivated Q235 steel samples to a controlled high-temperature environment (e.g., 750 °C) in a chloride salt atmosphere for varying durations. Perform X-ray diffraction and SEM analyses pre- and post-exposure to identify oxide phases and correlate these with weight loss measurements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature exposure does not lead to a detectable phase transformation in the passivation film or if the corrosion rate does not significantly increase in samples showing unchanged phase composition relative to room temperature, the hypothesis is falsified.

Liu et al. [] simulated the severe high-temperature corrosion environment of a pulverized coal boiler in a low-NOx combustion environment. The experimental results showed that the corrosion resistance of the prepared C22 laser-cladding layer was not only significantly better than that of 20 g steel, but also higher than that of a commercial C22 alloy of similar composition. In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.

papers.title: Research on the Corrosion Behavior of Q235 Pipeline Steel in an Atmospheric Environment through Experiment.
papers.system: Q235 low-carbon (pipeline) steel with an applied passivation film
papers.approach: Cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion experiments, weight loss measurements, and morphological/EDS analyses at ambient conditions
papers.findings: The study identified four distinct stages of corrosion – initial protective action of the passivation film, followed by film breakdown (with pitting and mixed rust formation), then a phase of matrix rust accumulation, and finally accelerated corrosion due to film rupture. EDS showed changes in elemental composition (loss of fluorine and increase in oxygen) correlating with film degradation.
papers.mechanism: Passivation film initially retards corrosion through an electrochemical barrier; however, upon exposure to chloride ions, the film starts to break down, leading to the formation of mixed oxides that, if not stabilized, allow aggressive attack and subsequent weight loss.

papers.title: Effective Corrosion Inhibition of Carbon Steel in Hydrochloric Acid by Dopamine-Produced Carbon Dots.
papers.system: Q235 (carbon) steel in 1 M HCl solution
papers.approach: Electrochemical measurements (EIS, potentiodynamic polarization) and weight loss studies with varying concentrations of nitrogen-doped carbon dots (NCDs) as inhibitors; tests conducted at room temperature and elevated temperatures between 298–328 K
papers.findings: NCDs act as a mixed-type inhibitor, forming an adsorbed protective film on the steel. Inhibition efficiency increased with NCD concentration, exposure time, and temperature, reaching about 96% at 400 ppm. The adsorption behavior obeys the Langmuir isotherm.
papers.mechanism: The formation of a stable and tightly adsorbed inhibitor film impedes corrosive species (e.g., H+ and Cl–) from attacking the steel, thus enhancing corrosion resistance.

papers.title: The Effect of Temperatures on the Passivation Behavior of Q235 Steel in the Simulated Concrete Pore Solution.
papers.system: Q235 steel in simulated concrete pore (SCP) solution
papers.approach: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and MS curve measurements at temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C to monitor the kinetics and characteristics of passive film formation
papers.findings: Passivation occurs in a rapid initial phase (within 24 h) followed by a steady state with the higher temperature accelerating film formation and favoring the production of more Fe3+ compounds; the passive film exhibits lower capacitance (indicating better protective properties) at higher temperatures.
papers.mechanism: Temperature elevation accelerates the growth rate and alters the composition of the passive film, enhancing its charge transfer resistance, but the film’s protective capability is contingent on achieving a stable, dense oxide layer.

papers.title: High-Temperature Corrosion of Ni-Cr-Mo Cladding Layers with Different Si Contents in NaCl-KCl-Na2SO4-K2SO4
papers.system: Q235 steel substrate with Ni-Cr-Mo cladding layers (with varied Si contents)
papers.approach: Laser cladding to deposit Ni-Cr-Mo alloy layers with different Si percentages, followed by weight loss measurements and microstructural analyses in molten salt environments at 550 °C
papers.findings: The addition of Si resulted in the formation of a dense chromium oxide film, which enhanced the high-temperature corrosion resistance. The cladding layer with 5 wt.% Si showed a significantly lower corrosion rate compared to that without Si.
papers.mechanism: Si promotes rapid and dense Cr2O3 formation, which serves as a barrier against aggressive species in high-temperature molten salt exposure. This dense oxide film mitigates corrosion-related degradation.

papers.title: An electrochemical study of pH influences on corrosion and passivation for a Q235 carbon steel in HNO3-NaNO2, HAc-NaNO2
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel in acidic electrolytes containing nitrite anions
papers.approach: Systematic electrochemical testing (polarization curves and EIS) across a range of pH values in different acid solutions
papers.findings: The study showed that passivation is possible within specific pH ranges, with the broadest passivation pH range observed in HNO3–NaNO2 solutions. Lower corrosion current densities and higher charge transfer resistances correlated with improved passivation. The film properties are influenced by both pH and the aggressive anions present.
papers.mechanism: Formation of passive oxide films is modulated by the interplay of nitrite’s oxidizing action and the solution pH, which determines the film’s composition and its ability to resist Cl– attack.

papers.title: Study on Synergistic Corrosion Inhibition Effect between Calcium Lignosulfonate (CLS) and Inorganic Inhibitors on Q235 Carbon Steel in Alkaline Environment
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel in alkaline solutions (pH ~11.5) with chloride ions
papers.approach: Immersion tests combined with cyclic potentiodynamic polarization, EIS, and SEM to evaluate the protective performance of hybrid inhibitors (CLS combined with inorganic inhibitors like molybdate, stannate, or tungstate)
papers.findings: The hybrid inhibitor, especially the CLS-molybdate combination, was most effective in forming a protective adsorption film, as indicated by high polarization resistance (Rp) and a reduced pitting susceptibility.
papers.mechanism: CLS molecules, aided by inorganic species, adsorb onto the steel surface and facilitate the formation of multilayer protection (passivation, deposition, adsorption), which minimizes Cl– involvement and retards corrosion.

established: A passivation film on Q235 steel initially offers electrochemical protection, but its integrity is compromised over time, especially in the presence of aggressive ions such as chloride.

Temperature influences passivation film kinetics – higher temperatures can accelerate both film formation (yielding denser, more protective layers in some cases) and film degradation due to thermal stress and spallation.
Protective mechanisms often involve the formation of stable oxides (e.g., Fe oxides, Cr2O3) or the maintenance of an adsorbed inhibitor layer that blocks corrosive attack.

approaches_tried.approach: Cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion testing and weight loss measurements on pre-passivated Q235 steel
approaches_tried.outcome: Identification of distinct corrosion stages and the role of the passivation film in delaying degradation; however, film rupture leads to eventual accelerated corrosion.

approaches_tried.approach: Electrochemical inhibition using adsorptive inhibitors (e.g., NCDs)
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated high inhibition efficiencies via stable adsorption films that reduce corrosion rates, particularly in acid solutions.

approaches_tried.approach: Temperature-controlled passivation studies in simulated concrete pore solutions
approaches_tried.outcome: Showed that elevated temperatures lead to faster film growth with altered composition, enhancing resistance under certain conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: High-temperature cladding (Ni-Cr-Mo with Si addition) on Q235 steel
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved high-temperature corrosion resistance through formation of dense, protective Cr-rich oxide layers.

mechanisms: Electrochemical barrier provided by a dense, adherent passive oxide film that prevents aggressive ion ingress.

Thermal effects influencing oxide film composition and integrity, where higher temperature may promote formation of more stable oxides (e.g., Fe3+ compounds or Cr2O3 in cladded layers) but can also induce film cracking via thermal stress.
Adsorption-based inhibition via organic or hybrid (organic/inorganic) layers that retard corrosion by occupying active sites.
disagreements: Some studies (e.g., in simulated pore solutions) report that elevated temperatures enhance passivation and protective film formation, whereas high-temperature exposure in aggressive molten salt environments or boiler conditions is associated with film spallation and accelerated degradation.
Differences exist regarding the durability of the passive film under varying pH and chloride concentrations, with certain acidic environments promoting more stable passivation than others.
open_questions: How does the intrinsic nature (composition and mechanical integrity) of the pre-exposure passivation film on Q235 steel control its long-term corrosion behavior under extreme high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C) compared to ambient conditions?
What is the threshold at which thermal stresses overcome the benefits of rapid passivation, leading to film rupture and accelerated degradation?
How might subsequent annealing or integration with high-entropy alloy coatings modify the stability and corrosion resistance mechanisms of the pre-formed passive films on Q235 steel?
opportunities: Design a controlled study that directly compares pre-passivated Q235 steel under two regimes: room temperature salt exposure versus high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure, with identical initial passivation treatments.

Investigate the evolution of the film microstructure (e.g., oxide phase and mechanical integrity) in situ using high-temperature electrochemical or spectroscopic methods to isolate the effect of thermal stress on film spallation.

Combine pre-exposure annealing treatments with passivation film characterization to assess whether thermal treatment can pre-stabilize the oxide layer, thereby extending its protective capacity under aggressive, high-temperature conditions.

Correlate quantitative changes in film properties (such as thickness, composition, and adherence) with corrosion kinetics to define a mechanistic model that predicts when and why protection fails; an observation of negligible film spallation or unchanged corrosion rates at high temperature relative to room temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of the pre-formed passivation film’s integrity under thermal expansion stresses, which at high temperatures may spall and expose the metal substrate.
directions.assessment: Directly attacks the core hypothesis that the protective film in its as-formed state can fail under high-temperature thermal mismatch; well supported by evidence showing film breakdown and weight-loss stages (PMC9504384::web::028, PMC9504384::web::017); feasible using combined salt-spray tests and high-temperature treatments with microscopy and impedance measurements.

directions.direction: Examine the impact of intrinsic microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., grain boundaries, inclusions) on localized chloride adsorption and subsequent corrosion, with the idea that such defects become more active under elevated temperatures.
directions.assessment: Attacks the limitation by isolating the role of localized defects on corrosion behavior that might differ between room and high-temperature regimes; supported indirectly by studies on passivation breakdown (PMC9504384) and can be isolated by comparing polished versus defect-engineered samples; feasible but requires high-resolution local measurements.

directions.direction: Study phase transformations in the passive film upon high-temperature exposure—from a dense, protective oxide (e.g., Fe3O4 or mixed passive products) to a more porous or non-protective phase—which would reduce corrosion resistance.
directions.assessment: Direct mechanistic focus on how the film’s chemical/phase structure evolves with temperature, addressing why protection persists at room temperature yet fails at 700–900 °C; supported by temperature-induced changes in oxide phases reported in PMC9867134 and analogous high-temperature studies (PMC9100067); experimental phase identification via XRD and SEM is feasible.

directions.direction: Evaluate whether thermally induced microcrack formation in the as-formed passivation film facilitates aggressive ion ingress (especially chloride) at high temperatures while leaving room-temperature performance largely unaffected.
directions.type: Processing/synthesis route with thermal cycling and surface characterization
directions.assessment: Targets the governing cause by isolating microcracking as the structural mediator; evidence from film rupture and bulging phenomena (PMC9504384::web::017, PMC9504384::web::028) supports the mechanism; feasibility is high with in situ high-temperature microscopy and impedance monitoring, and the approach respects the pre-exposure state of Q235 steel.

candidates.hypothesis: The protective pre-formed passivation film on Q235 steel degrades at high temperatures due to thermally induced microcracking initiated by rapid thermal cycling, thus permitting accelerated chloride ingress and corrosion compared to the intact film at ambient conditions.
candidates.intervention: Expose passivated samples to controlled, rapid thermal cycling (e.g., heating at 20 °C/min to 750 °C with a dwell time of 30 minutes, followed by rapid cooling) in a chloride salt-containing atmosphere versus continuous room-temperature exposure.
candidates.changes: Added explicit thermal cycling parameters (heating rate, dwell time, cooling rate, and number of cycles) for inducing microcracking. Clarified how microcrack formation differs from film spallation. References to literature on thermal-induced cracking in oxide films were included.

candidates.hypothesis: Thermal expansion mismatch between the pre-formed passivation film and the Q235 steel substrate causes spallation and microcracking at high temperatures, thereby compromising the film’s integrity and permitting aggressive ion ingress, in contrast to the intact film at room temperature.
candidates.intervention: Expose identical passivated samples to two regimes: a low-temperature (25 °C) chloride salt environment and a high-temperature (700–900 °C) environment designed to impose thermal expansion forces; the high-temperature protocol can involve steady heat or slow thermal ramping to allow stress build-up.
candidates.changes: Enhanced discussion of the thermal expansion mismatch by incorporating available material-property data and mentioning the potential influence of minor oxide phase evolution alongside spallation. Added clarification on expected spallation features and measurement techniques.

candidates.hypothesis: Upon exposure to high temperatures (700–900 °C), the originally protective passivation film on pre-exposed Q235 steel undergoes a phase transformation from a dense, Fe3O4-rich oxide to a more porous or non-stoichiometric oxide (e.g., FeO or mixed phases), resulting in a loss of adhesion and barrier properties and leading to accelerated corrosion compared to the stable oxide state maintained at room temperature.
candidates.intervention: Expose passivated Q235 steel samples to a controlled annealing process that mimics high-temperature exposure (e.g., ramp at 10 °C/min to 750 °C with a 30–60 minute hold) in a chloride salt atmosphere, compared to a control maintained at room temperature.
candidates.changes: Further detailed the expected phase transformation by explicitly naming specific oxide phases (e.g., transformation from a dense Fe3O4-rich film to a porous FeO or non-stoichiometric oxide) and included more precision regarding the annealing schedule. Added discussion of literature on phase transformation kinetics in iron oxide films under high-temperature chloride environments.

evidence_needs: Measurements of oxide-layer thickness evolution at different temperatures to confirm phase transformations with time.

minor_issues: Similar to Candidate A, the mechanism focuses on Fe3O4 → FeO transformations without exploring other iron oxide phases (e.g., Fe2O3) that may form at high temperatures.
